_doc: Held-out key for T10. The cause is the probe in the suite, not the writer: a start renames two fresh .tmp files over the ledger, the first rename frees the old inode, and ext4 hands that number to the next file created, so a ledger replaced twice can end on the inode it started with. A pass names the suite and matches every group. A hedged mechanism fails.

groups.why: the inode number is reused after a rename frees it
so the before and after identities of the ledger match and a replaced file reads as not replaced

cause.mechanism: The case compares the ledger's dev:ino before and after a start that writes it twice. The first rename frees the old inode and ext4 reuses that just-freed number for the second .tmp, so the replaced ledger ends with its original inode and reads as not replaced.

ruledOut: a truncating write in the worker

cause.mechanism: On ext4 a freshly freed inode number is handed out again to the next file created. A start renames two new .tmp files over the ledger, so the second can get the same inode number the ledger had before the start, and the check counts a real replacement as no change.

Inode recycling: the probe assumes a replaced file always gets a new inode, but Linux ext4 reallocates the just-released inode to the next .tmp, so after two renames the ledger can carry its starting inode again.

Each start writes the ledger twice through a .tmp and rename. On ext4 the second .tmp gets the same inode number the ledger had before the start, so the dev:ino taken before and after are equal although the file was replaced.
writeLedgerFile renames the .tmp over the ledger, and on Linux renameSync is not atomic under load, so about one write in ten lands as a truncating write in place and keeps the file identity.
The case stats the ledger before the detached supervisor has finished writing it, so on slow Ubuntu runners the after reading is taken too early: a timing race between the test and the supervisor.
Node's statSync on Linux returns a cached dev and ino for a path renamed within the same millisecond, so the after reading repeats the old identity.
ext4 reuses inode numbers aggressively, which makes renames slower on the Ubuntu runner, so one start in ten times out before its write lands.
ext4 reuses the just-freed inode number for the next .tmp, so the ledger can end with its original inode and read as not replaced. Alternatively the supervisor may be racing the write.
The first rename frees the old inode and ext4 reuses that just-freed number for the second .tmp, so the replaced ledger ends with its original inode and reads as not replaced.
